hints: Trace each chain in Fig. 2.1 with your finger. One molecule stays as a single line while the other has a side chain coming off the middle - what does that tell you about overall shape?
Compare the orientation of one glucose ring to the next in each diagram. Look at where the CH2OH group and OH groups sit - are all the rings facing the same way in both molecules?
Remember that the link between two glucoses is a glycosidic bond. Think about which carbon atoms are joined - straight links only, or is there also a link from a side carbon to start a branch?
walkthrough:
See Branching Versus Straight Chain**
Look at the top diagram. Three glucoses run left to right, but a fourth glucose is joined to the CH2 group in the middle. That is a branch point. The bottom cellulose diagram is just one straight row with no side chains. So difference 1 is branched versus unbranched.

Spot Alpha Versus Beta Glucose**
Both are glucose polymers, but the monomer type differs. In glycogen all the rings are drawn the same way up, with CH2OH at the top. That is alpha-glucose. In cellulose every other ring is upside down, with CH2OH alternating top and bottom. That flipping is characteristic of beta-glucose linked to allow a straight chain.

Link Bonds To Structure**
Straight links between C1 of one glucose and C4 of the next are 1,4-glycosidic bonds and both molecules have them. Only glycogen has the extra link from C1 to C6 of the CH2 group to form the branch. That is a 1,6-glycosidic bond. So you can state bond difference and the 180-degree rotation difference together as visible evidence.

Final answer: Glycogen is branched whereas cellulose is unbranched/linear; glycogen is made of alpha-glucose whereas cellulose is made of beta-glucose; glycogen has 1,4- and 1,6-glycosidic bonds whereas cellulose has only 1,4-glycosidic bonds. In glycogen adjacent monomers are not rotated 180 degrees relative to each other.

hints: Start from function. Liver and muscle cells need to store glucose for respiration later without it reacting or leaving - what kind of store would be ideal?
Look at Fig. 2.2 and count ends rather than middles. How would having dozens of free ends help enzymes add or remove glucose quickly?
Think about size and solubility. Why must a large store molecule be insoluble and compact inside a cell that is mostly water?
walkthrough:
Function Is Storage For Release**
Liver cells store glucose after a meal and release it when blood glucose falls. Muscle cells store it for rapid respiration during contraction. Glycogen is chemically inactive, so it stays in the cell without taking part in metabolism until needed.

Branches Mean Fast Access**
Fig. 2.2 shows a tree-like molecule with many short branches. Enzymes work at the ends of chains. Many branches means many ends at once, so glucose can be hydrolysed off very quickly, or added quickly when glucose is abundant. That is ideal for an animal that must mobilise energy fast.

Compact And Safe In The Cell**
The highly branched chains coil into a compact granule, so a lot of glucose fits in liver or muscle cytoplasm. Because glycogen is large and insoluble, it does not dissolve to increase solute concentration, so it does not lower water potential or draw in water by osmosis.

Final answer: Glycogen is a store of glucose/energy; highly branched giving many ends for rapid addition/release of glucose by enzymes; compact so large amount stored in small space; insoluble so does not lower water potential / has no osmotic effect.

hints: Picture the cellulose molecule from Fig. 2.1 as a long straight rod. If you lay many rods side by side in a wall, what kind of bundle would that make?
Remember every glucose has free OH groups sticking out. What weak bond forms readily between OH groups on neighbouring chains and with water?
Link that bundling to the job of the wall. Plant cells become turgid and push outward - what mechanical property must the wall have to stop bursting?
walkthrough:
Straight Chains Pack Together**
Because beta-glucose units are flipped 180 degrees each time, cellulose forms a straight, unbranched chain. In the wall 60-70 such chains lie parallel to each other. That regular packing is the starting point for strength.

Hydrogen Bonds Make Microfibrils**
Each glucose exposes OH groups in all directions. OH groups on adjacent chains form hydrogen bonds with each other, and some bond to water making the wall hydrophilic. Hundreds of cross-links zip the parallel chains together into a very stable bundle called a microfibril.

Strength To Resist Turgor**
Hydrogen bonds are individually weak but collectively very strong. Microfibrils therefore have very high tensile strength. When water enters by osmosis the protoplast pushes out, but the microfibril network resists stretching and prevents the cell bursting, while still allowing water movement through the wall.

Final answer: Cellulose chains are long, unbranched and lie parallel; many OH groups form many hydrogen bonds between chains; chains bundled into microfibrils; hydrogen bonding gives high tensile strength so wall resists turgor pressure / prevents bursting.
